Match on `store_id`, return `store_key`. On the Lookup's General page, set "Specify how to handle rows with no matching entries" to **Redirect rows to no match output** — not Fail Component, not Ignore Failure.

Route the no-match output to a Derived Column adding `error_description` = "Unresolved store_id," then an OLE DB Destination to a new review table, `stg.dim_store_unmatched`, so an unrecognized store ID is visible and investigable rather than vanishing.

## Step 5 — Resolve the product key with a Lookup against the current dimension row

Add a second Lookup against `dw.dim_product`:

```sql
SELECT product_key, sku FROM dw.dim_product WHERE is_current = 1;
```

Match on `sku`, return `product_key`. Same "Redirect rows to no match output" configuration, routed to `stg.dim_product_unmatched`. A SKU with no current match usually means a new product was sold before Riverside's product catalog process added it to `dim_product` — a real, recurring operational case, not a rare edge case, which is exactly why it needs a visible landing spot rather than a silent drop.

## Step 6 — Land the fully transformed rows in a clean staging-to-load table

Add a final OLE DB Destination writing successfully resolved rows (those that passed both Lookups) to `stg.stg_sales_ready_to_load` — a table shaped exactly like `dw.fact_sales` but still in the staging database, which is what Lesson 13's Load package reads from.

## Step 7 — Log the stage

Same pattern as Lesson 11: an Execute SQL Task writes to `stg.etl_run_log` with `stage = 'transform'`, including both the success-path row count and the no-match row counts from both Lookups — a non-zero no-match count should be visible in this log even on a night when the package otherwise reports success.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Transform package converts the raw staged strings to real types, calculates net_sales_amount using the exact formula enforced by the warehouse's check constraint, and resolves store and product natural keys via two Lookups — both explicitly configured to redirect no-match rows to review tables rather than fail or silently pass through a null key. That Lookup configuration is the one I'm flagging as worth double-checking in code review, since getting it wrong produces exactly the kind of silent data loss we investigate in Lesson 17.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The cleaning and matching step is built — this is where raw store exports get turned into the exact sales figures the business agreed on, and where we catch products or stores the system doesn't recognize yet instead of silently losing that data. One more SSIS stage (Load) and the pipeline is complete.
workplaceExplanation.executive: This step is where raw store data gets turned into the actual sales numbers you'll see — calculated the exact way your finance team confirmed, with returns and employee discounts already factored out — and it's built to flag anything unusual instead of quietly dropping it.

lessons.title: Building the SSIS Package: Load and Incremental Logic
lessons.summary: Loading only new transactions each night instead of reprocessing the whole history.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This is the final third of the nightly pipeline: Load. Clean, resolved rows sitting in `stg.stg_sales_ready_to_load` get written into `dw.fact_sales` — but only the previous day's new transactions, never the whole history, and in a way that's safe to re-run if someone needs to retry a night's load. We also close the loop on `dim_product`'s Type 2 logic, so a price change updates the dimension correctly instead of overwriting history.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine adding yesterday's receipts to a big filing cabinet that already has years of old receipts in it. You don't want to dump the whole filing cabinet out and start over every night — you just want to carefully add yesterday's stack. And if the power went out halfway through adding yesterday's stack and you have to try again, you want to make sure you don't accidentally end up with two copies of some of yesterday's receipts.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the incremental load pattern, and the two things that make it correct are the date-scoped insert and idempotency. The package loads only rows matching a specific `date_key` — the previous business day — rather than reprocessing the full staging history every night, which keeps runtime bounded regardless of how much history accumulates.

Idempotency is implemented with a delete-then-insert pattern scoped to the date being loaded: before inserting, the package deletes any existing `fact_sales` rows for that `date_key`. This means re-running the load for a given night — because someone fixed a bad file and wants to retry, exactly the Lesson 7 failure-recovery scenario — produces the same final state as running it once, never duplicated or double-counted rows. The `UQ_fact_sales_grain` constraint from Lesson 10 is a second line of defense here, not the primary mechanism — the delete-then-insert pattern is what makes retries safe by design, the constraint is what catches it if that logic ever has a bug.

We also close the Type 2 loop on `dim_product` here: when a product's price changes, the correct action is to expire the current row (set `expiration_date` and `is_current = 0`) and insert a new row with a new `product_key`, not update the existing row's price in place — that's what preserves the historical pricing Lesson 5 designed this dimension to support.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Create the Load package

Create `03_Load.dtsx`. This package has two responsibilities: maintaining `dim_product`'s Type 2 history, and loading `fact_sales` incrementally.

## Step 2 — Handle dim_product Type 2 changes first, before loading facts

Add a Data Flow comparing each resolved SKU's current price/category in `stg_sales_ready_to_load` against its current `dim_product` row (via a Lookup on `sku WHERE is_current = 1`). For any SKU where the price or category differs:

```sql
-- Expire the old version
UPDATE dw.dim_product
SET is_current = 0, expiration_date = DATEADD(DAY, -1, @LoadDate)
WHERE sku = @Sku AND is_current = 1;

-- Insert the new version
INSERT INTO dw.dim_product (sku, product_name, category, unit_price, is_current, effective_date, expiration_date)
VALUES (@Sku, @ProductName, @Category, @UnitPrice, 1, @LoadDate, NULL);
```

This is implemented as an Execute SQL Task parameterized per changed row (or a staged "changes" table processed in one set-based statement for better performance at scale) — either way, the old row is expired, never overwritten.

## Step 3 — Delete any existing fact rows for the date being loaded (idempotency)

```sql
DECLARE @LoadDateKey INT = (
    SELECT date_key FROM dw.dim_date WHERE full_date = @LoadDate
);

DELETE FROM dw.fact_sales WHERE date_key = @LoadDateKey;
```

Run this as an Execute SQL Task immediately before the insert, scoped to only the single date being loaded. This single statement is what makes re-running tonight's load after a fix completely safe — nothing else in the table for any other date is touched.

## Step 4 — Insert the resolved, deduplicated rows into fact_sales

Add a Data Flow Task: OLE DB Source reading `stg.stg_sales_ready_to_load` for the current `load_id`, joined against the now-current `dim_product` rows (re-resolving `product_key` in case Step 2 just created a new version), then an OLE DB Destination into `dw.fact_sales` using **fast load** mode with a reasonable batch size (e.g. 10,000 rows) for performance.

```sql
INSERT INTO dw.fact_sales
    (date_key, store_key, product_key, quantity_sold, gross_amount,
     return_amount, employee_discount_amount, net_sales_amount, load_id)
SELECT
    d.date_key, s.store_key, p.product_key,
    r.quantity, r.gross_amount, r.return_amount,
    r.employee_discount_amount, r.net_sales_amount, r.load_id
FROM stg.stg_sales_ready_to_load r
JOIN dw.dim_date d ON d.full_date = r.transaction_date
JOIN dw.dim_store s ON s.store_key = r.store_key
JOIN dw.dim_product p ON p.sku = r.sku AND p.is_current = 1
WHERE r.load_id = @LoadId;
```

## Step 5 — Verify the grain-level row count reconciles before declaring success

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS staged_ready,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dw.fact_sales WHERE load_id = @LoadId) AS loaded
FROM stg.stg_sales_ready_to_load
WHERE load_id = @LoadId;
-- both counts must match exactly
```

Wire this check as a precedence constraint: if the counts don't match, route to the same alerting path built in Lesson 7 instead of marking the run successful.

## Step 6 — Log final success and close out the load_batch row

```sql
UPDATE stg.load_batch SET files_received = files_received WHERE load_id = @LoadId;

INSERT INTO stg.etl_run_log (run_date, stage, status, rows_processed, started_at, completed_at)
VALUES (@LoadDate, 'load', 'success', @RowsLoaded, @StartTime, SYSDATETIME());
```

## Step 7 — Chain all three packages under one SQL Server Agent job

In SQL Server Agent, create a job "Riverside Nightly ETL" with three job steps — `01_Extract`, `02_Transform`, `03_Load` — each configured to go to the next step on success and jump to a final "On Failure" step (a Send Mail Task) if any step fails. Schedule it for 1:15am daily, exactly as planned in Lesson 6.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Load package handles dim_product's Type 2 changes first — expiring the old row and inserting a new one rather than overwriting price in place — then does a delete-then-insert scoped to the single date being loaded before the fact insert, which is what makes a retry idempotent. Added a row-count reconciliation check between staged-ready and loaded rows as the last gate before the run logs success. All three SSIS packages are now chained under one SQL Server Agent job scheduled for 1:15am.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The full nightly pipeline — extract, transform, load — is built and scheduled to run automatically every night ahead of the 9am deadline. This is the point where the data side of the project is functionally complete; the next lessons build the actual report and dashboard people will look at.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The automated nightly process is fully built and scheduled. Starting tonight, this replaces the manual Monday spreadsheet rebuild entirely — the numbers will already be sitting there, correct, before anyone opens their laptop.

lessons.title: Building the SSRS Paginated Report for Store Managers
lessons.summary: A single-store, print-friendly daily report, parameterized so each manager only sees their own numbers.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With the warehouse reliably filling every night, this lesson builds the first thing a Riverside employee actually sees: a single-store, parameterized SSRS paginated report that each of the 14 store managers opens every morning, showing only their own store's prior-day sales by product — exactly the "Delivery: SSRS report per store manager (their store only)" line from Lesson 1's requirements brief.
lessons.explainSimple: Think of a school where every student's report card is printed separately — a student only sees their own grades, not the whole school's. This report works the same way: each store manager opens one simple page every morning showing only their store's numbers from yesterday, not all 14 stores mixed together.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is a paginated report built in SQL Server Reporting Services, designed for exactly the use case paginated reporting is built for: a fixed, print-friendly layout, a single consumer-scoped view, and no interactive exploration required. The report's single dataset parameter, `@StoreId`, is what enforces data isolation — each store manager's subscription (configured at the end of this lesson) passes a fixed, hardcoded value of their own store's ID, so a given manager's version of the report is physically incapable of returning another store's rows, regardless of what they do with the rendered output.

The dataset query aggregates directly against `dw.fact_sales` joined to all three dimensions, filtered to the prior business day and the parameterized store. The report body uses a Tablix grouped by product category and sorted by net sales descending, which gives a store manager an immediate answer to "what moved and what didn't" without needing to sort or filter anything themselves — the entire point of a paginated report is that the layout does the organizing work the user would otherwise have to do themselves in an interactive tool.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Create the shared data source

In Report Builder (or SSDT's Reporting Services project), create a Shared Data Source pointed at `Riverside_DW` using a service account with read-only access — never a personal or admin credential, since this runs unattended on a schedule for every subscription.

## Step 2 — Write the dataset query with the StoreId parameter

```sql
SELECT
    p.category,
    p.product_name,
    SUM(f.quantity_sold)              AS units_sold,
    SUM(f.gross_amount)                 AS gross_amount,
    SUM(f.return_amount)                  AS return_amount,
    SUM(f.employee_discount_amount)         AS employee_discount_amount,
    SUM(f.net_sales_amount)                   AS net_sales_amount
FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_store s   ON s.store_key = f.store_key
JOIN dw.dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
JOIN dw.dim_date d    ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE s.store_id = @StoreId
  AND d.full_date = DATEADD(DAY, -1, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))
GROUP BY p.category, p.product_name
ORDER BY p.category, net_sales_amount DESC;
```

Create the `@StoreId` report parameter with no default and "Visible" turned off in the final published version -- it's meant to be supplied by the subscription, not typed in by the manager.

## Step 3 — Add a header showing the store and date being reported

Add a text box above the Tablix using an expression:

```
="Store " & Parameters!StoreId.Value & " -- Sales for " & Format(DateAdd("d", -1, Today()), "MMMM d, yyyy")
```

## Step 4 — Build the Tablix body, grouped by category

Insert a Tablix bound to the dataset. Add a row group on `category`, with detail rows showing `product_name`, `units_sold`, `gross_amount`, `return_amount`, `employee_discount_amount`, `net_sales_amount`. Add a subtotal row per category and a grand total row at the report's bottom, both using the Tablix's built-in Subtotal feature rather than a second query.

## Step 5 — Format for print, not for screen interaction

Set the report's page size to Letter, portrait, with a 0.5" margin, and confirm the Tablix's column widths fit within that width in the print layout preview — this report is explicitly meant to be printable, per the architecture decision in Lesson 4, not just viewed on a screen.

## Step 6 — Deploy to the Report Server and test with a real StoreId

Deploy the `.rdl` to the Reporting Services instance, then open it in the browser-based report viewer and manually supply `@StoreId = 'ST07'` to confirm it returns only Store 07's rows.

## Step 7 — Configure 14 data-driven subscriptions, one per store

In Report Manager, create a **data-driven subscription** using a query against `dw.dim_store` to generate one subscription per store, each passing that store's `store_id` as the fixed `@StoreId` parameter value and delivering to that store's manager's email address every morning at 7:30am — after the 7:00am load-completion checkpoint from Lesson 6, with 90 minutes of margin before the 9am store opening.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the SSRS paginated report against fact_sales, parameterized on StoreId with the parameter hidden in the published version. Data isolation is enforced at the subscription level — each of the 14 data-driven subscriptions passes a fixed, hardcoded store ID, so a given manager's delivered report can't return another store's rows. Deployed and scheduled for 7:30am delivery, after the load checkpoint and ahead of store opening.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Every store manager now gets an automatic email every morning with yesterday's numbers for their store specifically — no manual spreadsheet involved. This is the first deliverable in the brief that's fully live and in managers' inboxes, not just built.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Store managers are now getting their own store's numbers automatically every morning before the doors open, replacing whatever ad hoc process they had before. Each manager sees only their own store — this doesn't change anyone's visibility into other locations.

lessons.title: Building the Power BI Semantic Model on the Warehouse
lessons.summary: Modeling relationships and core DAX measures directly on top of the new star schema.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The store managers' report is live. Now we build the foundation of the VP of Operations' side of the platform: a Power BI semantic model connected directly to `Riverside_DW`, with the star schema's relationships modeled correctly and the core DAX measures written once, here, so every visual built in Lesson 16 — and any report anyone builds against this model in the future — calculates net sales, returns, and units sold exactly the same way.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine building a calculator just once and then handing it to everyone in the office, instead of letting every person build their own calculator that might add things up slightly differently. This lesson builds that one shared calculator — the measures for "total sales," "units sold," and so on — so that no matter which chart someone builds later, the numbers underneath are guaranteed to agree.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the semantic model layer: Power BI Desktop connected to `Riverside_DW` in Import mode (not DirectQuery — the reasoning for that choice is covered in full in Lesson 19, but the short version is that a nightly-refreshed dataset doesn't need query-time round trips to SQL Server on every click). We bring in all four warehouse tables and let Power BI's model view auto-detect relationships, then verify each one explicitly: `fact_sales` to each dimension should be a one-to-many relationship with a single filter direction flowing from the dimension to the fact table — never bidirectional, which would let a filter on one dimension ambiguously affect another dimension through the fact table, a problem we revisit directly in Lesson 19.

`dim_date` gets explicitly marked as the model's official **Date table** (Model view > right-click `dim_date` > Mark as date table, using `full_date` as the key column) — this one setting is what makes Power BI's time-intelligence DAX functions (`SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR`, `DATESYTD`, etc.) behave correctly, and skipping it is a common, hard-to-diagnose source of wrong year-over-year numbers. We then write the handful of foundational measures once, as explicit DAX using `CALCULATE` rather than implicit column aggregations, so every future visual references a named, auditable measure instead of a raw sum of a column.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Connect to the warehouse in Import mode

In Power BI Desktop: Get Data > SQL Server, server and database for `Riverside_DW`, Import mode (not DirectQuery). Select all four tables: `dw.dim_date`, `dw.dim_store`, `dw.dim_product`, `dw.fact_sales`.

## Step 2 — Verify every relationship explicitly in Model view

Confirm four relationships exist, each one-to-many with a single (not bidirectional) filter direction from dimension to fact:

```
dim_date (1)   --> (many) fact_sales   on date_key
dim_store (1)  --> (many) fact_sales   on store_key
dim_product (1) --> (many) fact_sales   on product_key
```

If Power BI auto-detected any relationship as bidirectional, change it to single-direction manually -- a star schema should almost never need bidirectional filtering, and leaving it on "both" is a common source of ambiguous or unexpectedly slow results later.

## Step 3 — Mark dim_date as the official Date table

Model view > right-click `dim_date` > **Mark as date table**, select `full_date` as the date column. Confirm there are no gaps in the date range relative to the data actually in `fact_sales`.

## Step 4 — Write the core measures in a dedicated measure table

Create a blank table (New Table with no rows, or a disconnected table) named `_Measures` to keep every measure organized in one place rather than scattered across the physical tables:

```dax
Total Net Sales =
SUM ( dw.fact_sales[net_sales_amount] )

Total Gross Sales =
SUM ( dw.fact_sales[gross_amount] )

Total Units Sold =
SUM ( dw.fact_sales[quantity_sold] )

Total Returns =
SUM ( dw.fact_sales[return_amount] )

Return Rate =
DIVIDE ( [Total Returns], [Total Gross Sales], 0 )
```

## Step 5 — Add the time-intelligence measures the VP's trailing-week and YoY views depend on

```dax
Net Sales Prior Year =
CALCULATE ( [Total Net Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( dw.dim_date[full_date] ) )

Net Sales YoY % =
DIVIDE ( [Total Net Sales] - [Net Sales Prior Year], [Net Sales Prior Year], 0 )

Net Sales Trailing 7 Days =
CALCULATE (
    [Total Net Sales],
    DATESINPERIOD ( dw.dim_date[full_date], MAX ( dw.dim_date[full_date] ), -7, DAY )
)
```

`SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` and `DATESINPERIOD` only produce correct results because `dim_date` was explicitly marked as a date table in Step 3 -- skipping that step is the single most common reason these exact functions silently return wrong numbers.

## Step 6 — Confirm a measure against a known value before building any visuals

Build a single quick card visual with `[Total Net Sales]` filtered to one store and one specific day, and compare it by hand against the SSRS report for that same store and day from Lesson 14 -- both should agree to the cent. This is a small, cheap version of the full reconciliation you'll formalize in Lesson 18.

## Step 7 — Set the refresh schedule

In the Power BI service, after publishing, configure a Scheduled Refresh for 7:15am daily -- after the 7:00am load-completion checkpoint, with enough margin before the VP's typical start of day.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the semantic model in Import mode with all four warehouse relationships verified as single-direction, and dim_date explicitly marked as the model's date table — that setting is what makes the YoY and trailing-week measures calculate correctly. Core measures are centralized in a dedicated _Measures table using CALCULATE rather than implicit aggregations, and I spot-checked Total Net Sales against the SSRS report for one store/day before building any visuals.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The analytical foundation for the VP's dashboard is built and the core calculations are defined once, centrally, so every chart built in the next lesson is guaranteed to agree with every other chart and with the store managers' report. Scheduled refresh is configured to run right after the nightly data load finishes.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built the calculation engine behind your dashboard — the part that defines what 'total sales' and 'year-over-year' actually mean — and confirmed it matches a store manager's report exactly before building anything visual on top of it.

lessons.title: Building the Power BI Executive Dashboard
lessons.summary: A 14-store rollup view built for the VP of Operations' morning routine.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The semantic model is verified and trustworthy. This lesson builds what the VP of Operations actually opens every morning: a single-page Power BI dashboard rolling up all 14 stores at once, built around her stated routine from the Lesson 1 discovery meeting — "I look at all 14 together" — with the ability to drill into any one store without leaving the page.
lessons.explainSimple: Think of a scoreboard at a sports tournament with 14 teams on it at once, so the coach can see how everyone's doing in one glance — and if one team looks interesting, the coach can tap on it to see more detail about just that team. That's what this dashboard does for the VP: all 14 stores in one glance, with the ability to zoom into any single one.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is dashboard design for a specific, known user and a specific, known routine, not a generic exploration tool — the VP described checking this before her first meeting, which means the default view on open has to answer her core question with zero clicks. The layout leads with KPI cards for `[Total Net Sales]`, `[Net Sales Trailing 7 Days]`, and `[Net Sales YoY %]` at the top, using conditional formatting (a built-in rule, not a manually colored text box) to flag the YoY card red when negative.

Below that, a matrix visual with stores as rows and `[Total Net Sales]` / `[Net Sales YoY %]` as columns gives the all-14-at-once view she asked for directly, sorted descending by net sales so underperformers surface near the bottom without her having to sort manually. A trend line chart of `[Total Net Sales]` by day over the trailing 8 weeks, and a bar chart by product category, round out the page. Drill-through is implemented as a dedicated hidden "Store Detail" page receiving a cross-filter when the VP right-clicks a row in the matrix and selects Drill through — giving her a single-store deep-dive without needing a second report or a second tool, directly fulfilling the "ability to drill into a single store" acceptance criterion from Lesson 2.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Lay out the page around the VP's stated morning routine, not a generic template

Reserve the top strip for three KPI cards, the middle-left for the 14-store matrix, the middle-right for the trend line, and the bottom for the category breakdown -- in that priority order, since the KPI cards need to be visible without any scrolling on her standard laptop screen.

## Step 2 — Build the KPI card row with conditional formatting

Add three Card visuals: `[Total Net Sales]`, `[Net Sales Trailing 7 Days]`, `[Net Sales YoY %]`. On the YoY card, open Conditional Formatting > Font Color, set a rule: value < 0 renders in the platform's warning red, value >= 0 in standard dark text -- using the built-in rules engine, not a manually set static color, so it updates automatically as the data changes.

## Step 3 — Build the 14-store matrix as the dashboard's centerpiece

Add a Matrix visual: Rows = `dim_store[store_name]`, Values = `[Total Net Sales]`, `[Net Sales YoY %]`. Sort by `[Total Net Sales]` descending. Apply conditional formatting as data bars on the net sales column so relative performance is visible at a glance across all 14 rows without reading every number.

## Step 4 — Add the trailing trend line

Add a Line Chart: Axis = `dim_date[full_date]` (filtered to the trailing 8 weeks via a visual-level filter), Values = `[Total Net Sales]`. This answers "is this a one-day blip or a real trend" at a glance, which matters directly for Lesson 20's interpretation work.

## Step 5 — Add the category breakdown

Add a Bar Chart: Axis = `dim_product[category]`, Values = `[Total Net Sales]`, sorted descending -- giving the VP the product-mix view the original discovery meeting flagged as something the old manual spreadsheet couldn't show at all.

## Step 6 — Build the hidden Store Detail drill-through page

Add a new page, "Store Detail," with a `dim_store[store_name]` field added to the Drillthrough well in the Visualizations pane. Add a table of `dim_product[product_name]` by `[Total Net Sales]` and `[Total Units Sold]`, plus a "Back" button (Insert > Buttons > Back). Hide this page from the page navigation (right-click the page tab > Hide Page) so it's only reachable via drill-through, keeping the main page uncluttered.

## Step 7 — Test the drill-through and publish

On the main page's matrix, right-click any single store's row > Drill through > Store Detail, and confirm it filters correctly to just that store. Publish to the Power BI service workspace, confirm the Lesson 15 scheduled refresh still applies to the published dataset, and share the report with the VP's account specifically (not a broad workspace share) per the platform's row-level access expectations.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the executive dashboard around the exact routine the VP described in discovery: KPI cards with conditional formatting up top, a sortable 14-store matrix as the centerpiece, an 8-week trend line, and a category breakdown — all driven off the measures from the Lesson 15 semantic model, nothing recalculated locally. Drill-through to a hidden single-store detail page covers the 'drill into one store' acceptance criterion from Lesson 2 without needing a second report.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The executive dashboard is built and matches the acceptance criteria from early in the project — all 14 stores visible at once, with drill-down into any single store. This closes out the implementation phase; next we move into validating everything actually works correctly before calling it done.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Your dashboard is built around exactly the morning routine you described in our first conversation — everything you need to see across all 14 stores in one glance, with the ability to click into any single store for more detail. Before this goes live for good, we're going to stress-test it to make sure every number holds up.

lessons.title: When the SSIS Load Silently Drops Rows
lessons.summary: Diagnosing a load that reports success but is quietly missing data.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The platform looks finished, but "looks finished" and "is correct" are different claims — this lesson proves it with a real bug. During validation, Store 11's numbers come in consistently lower than expected, even though the nightly SSIS job has reported "Success" every single night. We trace it down to the exact failure mode the fail-loud design in Lesson 7 was supposed to prevent, and fix it.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a mail sorter that's supposed to put every letter into one of 14 mailboxes, and if a letter doesn't fit any mailbox, drop it into a special "needs review" bin so someone notices. Now imagine that special bin doesn't actually exist — so any letter that doesn't fit just falls on the floor behind the sorting machine, where nobody can see it, while the sorter cheerfully reports "all letters sorted successfully!" That's the bug: the machine isn't lying exactly, it's just not looking at the floor.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The symptom: `stg.etl_run_log` shows `status = 'success'` for Store 11 every night, but a manual comparison against the raw CSV export shows roughly 6% of Store 11's transactions missing from `dw.fact_sales` on any given day. The package isn't failing — it's succeeding while quietly losing data, which is exactly the failure mode the Lesson 7 design philosophy ("never invisible") was meant to rule out everywhere.

The root cause is in the Transform package's product Lookup, built in Lesson 12: the Lookup transformation was correctly configured to "Redirect rows to no match output," but the no-match output was wired to an OLE DB Destination pointed at `stg.dim_product_unmatched` — except that table was created with a schema mismatch (missing a column SSIS expected), so every write to it silently failed at the component level and SSIS, per its default error handling on that specific destination, was configured to continue rather than fail the Data Flow. Store 11 happens to carry a regional house brand with SKUs that were onboarded into the POS system before anyone added them to `dim_product`, so a meaningful share of its transactions were hitting the broken no-match path every single night. The fix touches two layers: correct the `dim_product_unmatched` table schema so the error path actually works, and — more importantly — change the OLE DB Destination's error handling so a failure writing to the *error table itself* fails the package loudly, because an error-handling path that can itself fail silently defeats the entire point of having one.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Don't trust "Success" — reconcile a raw count first

```sql
-- Count raw rows that landed in staging for Store 11, one specific night
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg.stg_pos_transactions
WHERE store_id_raw = 'ST11' AND load_id = @SuspectLoadId;

-- Count rows that actually made it into the fact table for that same night
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
WHERE s.store_id = 'ST11' AND f.load_id = @SuspectLoadId;
```

The two counts don't match -- roughly 6% of rows are missing, and `stg.etl_run_log` shows no failure anywhere. This confirms the bug is real and rules out "the file was just short that night."

## Step 2 — Check the no-match review tables first, since that's where resolution failures should land

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg.dim_product_unmatched WHERE load_id = @SuspectLoadId;
-- Returns 0 -- but we KNOW rows are missing. A healthy-looking empty table
-- here is itself the red flag: it's either truly empty, or it's not being
-- written to at all.
```

## Step 3 — Check the SSIS execution log for the Transform package, not just the custom etl_run_log

Open the package execution report in SSISDB (`Integration Services Catalogs > SSISDB > right-click the execution > Overview/All Messages`). Buried in the component-level messages, not the package-level status, is a warning: the OLE DB Destination writing to `stg.dim_product_unmatched` failed with a column-count mismatch, and its `FailParentOnError` property was left at its default of `False` -- so the Data Flow logged the warning and moved on, and the package-level status still reported Success.

## Step 4 — Confirm the actual schema mismatch

```sql
-- The Lookup's no-match output includes an error_description column
-- that the destination table was never built with:
SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = 'stg' AND TABLE_NAME = 'dim_product_unmatched';
-- error_description is missing from the actual table
```

## Step 5 — Fix the table schema

```sql
ALTER TABLE stg.dim_product_unmatched
ADD error_description NVARCHAR(1000) NULL;
```

## Step 6 — Fix the real root cause: make the error path itself fail loudly if it breaks

In the OLE DB Destination writing to `stg.dim_product_unmatched`, set `FailParentOnError` to `True`, and on the Data Flow Task itself, remove any "continue on error" override at the task level. The goal is simple: if the mechanism meant to catch and surface a problem fails itself, the whole package should stop and alert -- not quietly degrade into exactly the silent-loss scenario it exists to prevent.

## Step 7 — Re-run the night in question and reconcile again

After the fix, re-run the Transform and Load packages for the affected date (safe, because Lesson 13's delete-then-insert pattern makes this idempotent), and re-run the Step 1 reconciliation query. Counts should now match, and `stg.dim_product_unmatched` should show the real set of unresolved Store 11 SKUs -- which gets handed to Riverside's merchandising team to add to the product catalog, closing the loop on the actual data problem underneath the bug.

## Step 8 — Add a regression check for this specific failure mode

```sql
-- Run nightly, alert if this ever returns non-zero unexpectedly without
-- a corresponding, reviewed entry in dim_product_unmatched / dim_store_unmatched:
SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg.stg_sales_ready_to_load WHERE load_id = @LoadId) +
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg.dim_product_unmatched WHERE load_id = @LoadId) +
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg.dim_store_unmatched WHERE load_id = @LoadId)
    AS accounted_for_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg.stg_pos_transactions WHERE load_id = @LoadId) AS total_staged;
-- these two numbers must always match: every staged row must be accounted
-- for in exactly one of (loaded, product-unmatched, store-unmatched)
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Found and fixed a silent data-loss bug in the Transform package. The product Lookup's no-match output was correctly redirected, but the destination table it wrote to had a schema mismatch that made every write to it fail silently, because FailParentOnError was left at its default False — so the package kept reporting Success while losing roughly 6% of Store 11's rows nightly. Fixed the table schema, set FailParentOnError to True on that destination, re-ran the affected date, and added a row-accounting check that alerts if staged, loaded, and unmatched counts ever stop reconciling to the total.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We caught and fixed a real data-quality bug during validation — Store 11 was quietly undercounted for several nights due to a gap in our own error-handling logic, not a problem with the store's data itself. It's fixed, the affected nights are corrected, and we've added an automatic check specifically designed to catch this exact failure mode again if it ever recurs.
workplaceExplanation.executive: During our own internal testing, we found and fixed an issue that was understating Store 11's sales by about 6% on the nights it occurred. It never reached a report you saw, it's corrected, and we've added a safeguard specifically aimed at this failure mode so it can't happen silently again.

lessons.title: Reconciling Power BI Totals Against the Source System
lessons.summary: Proving the dashboard's numbers actually match the POS exports before anyone trusts them.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Fixing one bug isn't the same as proving the whole platform is trustworthy. This lesson builds a formal, repeatable reconciliation process that proves the Power BI dashboard's totals match the original POS exports — directly fulfilling acceptance criterion AC-7 from Lesson 2 — and turns it into part of the standing UAT sign-off process, not a one-time check.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you count a jar of marbles by hand, and then you also use a marble-counting machine. Before you trust the machine from now on, you'd want to count the same jar both ways a few times and make sure you always get the same number. That's reconciliation — proving the automatic system agrees with counting it the slow, manual way, before you stop double-checking it every time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Reconciliation here means tracing a number from the dashboard all the way back to the original, untouched source file, through every transformation in between, and confirming it ties out at each hop — not just checking the final total in isolation, since a final total can accidentally match even when the underlying logic is wrong (two offsetting errors, for instance). The three checkpoints are: raw CSV total, staging table total, and `fact_sales` / Power BI total, each compared for the same store and date.

This needs to be a repeatable, documented procedure, not an ad hoc query run once during UAT and forgotten — because the real value isn't the one-time proof, it's having a known-good process ready the first time someone (reasonably) asks "are you sure these numbers are right?" months after launch. We also deliberately pick several different kinds of days to test against — an ordinary day, a day with returns, a day with employee discounts, and a day for a store that had a data-quality issue caught in Lesson 17 — because a reconciliation check that only ever runs against simple, clean days doesn't actually prove the edge cases work.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pick a representative sample of days and stores, not just one easy case

```
TEST CASE 1: Store 03, an ordinary weekday -- baseline check
TEST CASE 2: Store 05, a day with several returns -- tests return_amount logic
TEST CASE 3: Store 09, a day with employee discounts recorded -- tests
             employee_discount_amount logic
TEST CASE 4: Store 11, a night from the Lesson 17 bug window, post-fix --
             confirms the fix actually holds
```

## Step 2 — Compute the raw source total directly from the original CSV

For each test case, open that night's original CSV export (archived by the File System Task built in Lesson 11) and compute the expected net sales by hand, in Excel or a quick script, using the exact same formula as the warehouse: `SUM(quantity * unit_price) - SUM(return amounts) - SUM(employee discount amounts)`.

## Step 3 — Compute the same total from the staging table

```sql
SELECT
    SUM(CAST(quantity_raw AS INT) * CAST(unit_price_raw AS DECIMAL(10,2)))
        - SUM(CASE WHEN is_return_raw = 'TRUE'
                    THEN CAST(quantity_raw AS INT) * CAST(unit_price_raw AS DECIMAL(10,2))
                    ELSE 0 END)
        - SUM(CASE WHEN discount_type_raw = 'EMPLOYEE'
                    THEN CAST(discount_amount_raw AS DECIMAL(10,2)) ELSE 0 END)
        AS computed_net_sales
FROM stg.stg_pos_transactions
WHERE store_id_raw = @TestStoreId AND transaction_date_raw = @TestDate;
```

This should match Step 2 exactly -- if it doesn't, the bug is in Extract (Lesson 11), not Transform or Load.

## Step 4 — Compute the same total from the warehouse

```sql
SELECT SUM(net_sales_amount) AS warehouse_net_sales
FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
JOIN dw.dim_date d  ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE s.store_id = @TestStoreId AND d.full_date = @TestDate;
```

This should match Step 3 -- if it doesn't, the bug is in Load (Lesson 13) or in how Transform (Lesson 12) resolved dimension keys.

## Step 5 — Compute the same total directly in Power BI

Open the published dashboard, filter the Store Detail drill-through page (built in Lesson 16) to the test store and date using a visual-level filter, and read `[Total Net Sales]` off a card. This should match Step 4 -- if it doesn't, the bug is in the DAX measure or the model's relationships (Lesson 15), not the warehouse.

## Step 6 — Document every hop in a reconciliation worksheet, not just the pass/fail result

```
TEST CASE          CSV TOTAL    STAGING TOTAL   WAREHOUSE TOTAL   POWER BI TOTAL   MATCH?
Store 03, 10/14     $4,218.50    $4,218.50        $4,218.50          $4,218.50        YES
Store 05, 10/15     $3,904.75    $3,904.75        $3,904.75          $3,904.75        YES
Store 09, 10/16     $5,102.20    $5,102.20        $5,102.20          $5,102.20        YES
Store 11, 10/20     $3,311.00    $3,311.00        $3,311.00          $3,311.00        YES (post-fix)
```

Keeping all four columns, not just a final yes/no, is what makes this worksheet useful for diagnosing where a future mismatch originates, not just whether one exists.

## Step 7 — Make this a repeatable step in the UAT sign-off, not a one-time proof

Add "Reconciliation worksheet attached and all rows match" as a literal line item on the UAT sign-off checklist that gets presented in Lesson 22, and keep the query templates from Steps 2 through 5 saved so this exact check can be re-run any time trust in a number needs to be re-established.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built and ran a four-hop reconciliation — raw CSV, staging, warehouse, Power BI — across four representative test cases including an ordinary day, a returns-heavy day, an employee-discount day, and the Store 11 night from the Lesson 17 fix. Every hop ties out exactly. Saved the query templates so this isn't a one-time proof — it's a repeatable check we can rerun whenever trust in a number needs re-establishing.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've formally proven the dashboard's numbers match the original store data, tracing it through every step of the pipeline, not just checking the final total. This becomes a standing line item in UAT sign-off, so 'are these numbers right' has a documented, repeatable answer going forward.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We independently verified that every number on your dashboard ties back exactly to your stores' original sales records, across several different kinds of days including ones with returns and employee discounts. This is the proof step before we call the numbers trustworthy enough to run the business on.

lessons.title: Why the Dashboard Was Slow, and How We Fixed It
lessons.summary: Finding and fixing a real performance problem in the data model, not just the visuals.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The numbers are proven correct — now we fix a real performance problem. During UAT, the VP reports that clicking a store in the matrix to drill through takes 8–10 seconds, which is noticeably sluggish for a dashboard meant to be checked quickly every morning. This lesson diagnoses the actual cause in the data model, not just the visuals, and fixes it.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a library where, every single time someone asks "how many mystery books do we have?", a librarian has to walk through every single shelf in the whole building and count one by one, instead of checking a sign that already says the total. That's slow, and it gets slower every time the library adds more books. The fix isn't a faster librarian — it's keeping an already-updated sign so nobody has to recount the whole building every time someone asks.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The instinct when a dashboard feels slow is to blame the visuals, but the actual bottleneck is almost always in the model or the query, and that's exactly the case here. Using Power BI Desktop's **Performance Analyzer** (View ribbon > Performance Analyzer > Start Recording > Refresh Visuals), we capture the time breakdown for the slow drill-through interaction and find the vast majority of the 8-10 seconds is in the "DAX query" phase for the Store Detail table visual, not rendering.

Digging into the DAX, the `[Total Units Sold]` measure on the Store Detail page was written using a row-by-row `SUMX` wrapped around a nested `FILTER(ALL(dw.fact_sales), ...)` pattern rather than a simple `CALCULATE(SUM(...))` — a holdover from an earlier draft that bypassed the model's relationships to filter the fact table manually, forcing the formula engine to evaluate row-by-row over the full table instead of letting the storage engine execute a set-based aggregation. The fix is to rewrite the measure as a plain `CALCULATE` + `SUM` that relies on the model's existing single-direction relationships (verified back in Lesson 15) to do the filtering, which lets Power BI push the aggregation down to the fast, columnar storage engine instead of the much slower formula engine.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Measure before guessing: run Performance Analyzer

In Power BI Desktop, open the Store Detail page, go to View > Performance Analyzer > Start Recording, then click Refresh Visuals and perform the drill-through interaction that felt slow. Expand each visual's entry in the Performance Analyzer pane.

```
Table visual ("Product detail"): 7,840ms total
  DAX query:      7,310ms   <-- the actual bottleneck
  Visual display:   410ms
  Other:             120ms
```

This immediately rules out "the visuals are too complex" -- the problem is the query feeding the table, not the rendering.

## Step 2 — Copy the slow query into DAX Studio for a closer look

Right-click the entry in Performance Analyzer > "Copy query," paste it into DAX Studio (a free external tool), and run Server Timing to see the formula-engine vs. storage-engine split.

```
FE (Formula Engine): 7,100ms   <-- almost all of the time
SE (Storage Engine):   180ms
```

A query that's almost entirely formula-engine time, for a simple aggregation, is the classic signature of row-by-row evaluation instead of a set-based operation.

## Step 3 — Find the offending measure

```dax
-- BEFORE (the slow version):
Total Units Sold =
SUMX (
    FILTER (
        ALL ( dw.fact_sales ),
        dw.fact_sales[store_key] = SELECTEDVALUE ( dw.dim_store[store_key] )
    ),
    dw.fact_sales[quantity_sold]
)
```

This wraps `ALL(dw.fact_sales)` -- explicitly ignoring the model's relationships and filter context -- and then manually re-filters row by row with `FILTER` and `SUMX`, forcing the formula engine to iterate the entire fact table for every single row of the visual instead of letting the relationships and the storage engine do it in one set-based pass.

## Step 4 — Rewrite it to use the model's relationships instead of fighting them

```dax
-- AFTER (the fast version):
Total Units Sold =
CALCULATE ( SUM ( dw.fact_sales[quantity_sold] ) )
```

Because the `dim_store` -> `fact_sales` relationship (verified single-direction back in Lesson 15) already filters `fact_sales` down to the selected store whenever a store is in the filter context, `CALCULATE(SUM(...))` gets exactly the right rows without the model ever needing to be overridden or manually re-filtered.

## Step 5 — Re-run Performance Analyzer and confirm the fix

```
Table visual ("Product detail"): 240ms total
  DAX query:       95ms
  Visual display:  130ms
  Other:            15ms
```

Down from ~7,840ms to ~240ms -- a roughly 30x improvement, entirely from the DAX rewrite, with zero changes to the visual itself.

## Step 6 — Audit every other measure in the model for the same pattern

```dax
-- Search the model for any measure using this anti-pattern:
-- SUMX( FILTER( ALL(...) or ALLSELECTED(...), ... ), ... )
-- when a simple CALCULATE(SUM(...)) relying on existing relationships
-- would produce the same result.
```

In this case, `[Total Net Sales]`, `[Total Gross Sales]`, and the time-intelligence measures from Lesson 15 were all already written correctly using `CALCULATE` -- only this one measure, added later during Lesson 16's build, had the anti-pattern, which is a useful reminder that a performance regression can be introduced by a single measure even in an otherwise well-built model.

## Step 7 — Document the finding for future maintainers

Add a comment directly on the measure in Power BI Desktop (right-click the measure > Properties > Description): "Rewritten 10/2026 -- avoid SUMX(FILTER(ALL(...))) patterns; let model relationships handle filtering." This is exactly the kind of note that belongs in Lesson 23's handoff documentation too.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Used Performance Analyzer and DAX Studio to confirm the slow drill-through was almost entirely formula-engine time, not rendering or network. Root cause was a Total Units Sold measure using SUMX(FILTER(ALL(fact_sales),...)) — bypassing the model's relationships and forcing row-by-row evaluation. Rewrote it as a plain CALCULATE(SUM(...)) that lets the existing single-direction relationships do the filtering, cutting that query from ~7.8 seconds to ~240ms. Audited the rest of the model's measures for the same pattern; nothing else needed changing.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We found and fixed the cause of the slow drill-through the VP flagged during testing — it was a calculation written inefficiently, not a hardware or data-volume problem. It's now about 30 times faster, and we checked the rest of the dashboard's calculations for the same issue so it doesn't resurface elsewhere.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The slow drill-through you noticed during testing is fixed — it now responds almost instantly. The cause was a calculation that needed to be rewritten more efficiently, not a sign of a bigger problem, and we checked the rest of the dashboard to make sure nothing similar is lurking elsewhere.

lessons.title: Reading the First Real Numbers: What the Dashboard Told the Business
lessons.summary: Interpreting the first live week of data, not just verifying it's technically correct.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The platform is technically correct and fast. This lesson is about the skill that's easy to skip but actually separates a BI developer from someone who just knows the tools: sitting down with the first full week of real, live data and interpreting it — not just confirming it loaded correctly, but reading what it's actually saying, and being honest about what one week can and can't tell you.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you just got a thermometer that tells you the temperature outside, and on its first day it says it's unusually cold. Does that mean winter is coming early, or was it just one cold day? You can't tell from one reading alone — you'd want to watch it for a while before deciding anything. That's the skill in this lesson: looking at the first week of real numbers carefully, without jumping to a big conclusion that one week alone can't actually support.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the difference between data validation (does the number match the source — covered in Lesson 18) and data interpretation (what does the number mean for the business — the actual point of building the platform at all). The first live week shows two things worth flagging to the VP: Store 06 is roughly 18% below the 14-store average in net sales per day, and the "Outdoor Cooking" product category is the fastest-growing category week-over-week across nearly every store.

The interpretation discipline here is distinguishing signal from noise with the amount of data actually in hand. One week is enough to notice a pattern worth watching; it is not enough to declare Store 06 "underperforming" as a settled fact, because a single slow week could be a one-off (a nearby road closure, a staffing gap, a local competitor's sale) rather than a sustained trend. The responsible move is to present both findings with an explicit confidence qualifier attached to each — "worth watching, confirm after 4 weeks" versus "consistent enough across stores to act on now" — rather than presenting every number with the same false certainty just because the dashboard renders them all in the same clean font.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull the first full week's numbers and look for the real headline, not every number

```sql
SELECT s.store_name, SUM(f.net_sales_amount) AS week_net_sales,
       SUM(f.net_sales_amount) / 7.0 AS avg_daily_net_sales
FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
JOIN dw.dim_date d  ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE d.full_date BETWEEN @WeekStart AND @WeekEnd
GROUP BY s.store_name
ORDER BY avg_daily_net_sales ASC;
```

Store 06 sits noticeably below the other 13 -- about 18% under the 14-store average daily net sales for the week.

## Step 2 — Check the category breakdown for a second, independent signal

```sql
SELECT p.category, SUM(f.net_sales_amount) AS week_net_sales
FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_product p ON p.product_key = f.product_key
JOIN dw.dim_date d    ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE d.full_date BETWEEN @WeekStart AND @WeekEnd
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY week_net_sales DESC;
```

"Outdoor Cooking" shows the largest week-over-week growth rate of any category, and it's consistent across most of the 14 stores -- not driven by one outlier location.

## Step 3 — Apply an honest confidence level to each finding before writing anything down

```
FINDING 1: Store 06 is ~18% below average for the week.
CONFIDENCE: Low -- one week of data. Could be a real issue (staffing,
local competition, a closed road) or noise (one unusual week).
RECOMMENDED ACTION: Watch for 3-4 more weeks before concluding anything;
flag it now so the VP isn't surprised later if it persists.

FINDING 2: "Outdoor Cooking" category is growing fastest, consistently
across stores.
CONFIDENCE: Moderate-to-high -- the pattern repeats across most of the
14 stores independently, which is much stronger evidence than a single
store's single-week number.
RECOMMENDED ACTION: Worth raising to merchandising/buying now, since
the consistency across locations makes this unlikely to be noise.
```

## Step 4 — Write the finding up with the confidence level attached, explicitly

Never present a one-week number with the same confident tone a four-week trend deserves. Draft the actual language you'll use in the conversation:

```
"Two things stood out in the first full week. First, Store 06 is running
about 18% below the other stores -- it's one week of data, so I wouldn't
read too much into it yet, but I'm flagging it now so we're watching it
together rather than discovering it later. Second, and I'd put more
weight on this one because it's consistent across almost every store:
Outdoor Cooking is your fastest-growing category this week. That seems
worth a conversation with merchandising sooner rather than later."
```

## Step 5 — Set a concrete follow-up trigger, not a vague "we'll keep an eye on it"

Agree with the VP on a specific re-check point: "Let's look at Store 06 again after week 4 of live data — if it's still 15%+ below average by then, that's worth investigating directly rather than waiting." A vague promise to monitor something tends to quietly never get revisited; a specific date and threshold does.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Pulled the first live week's numbers and found two patterns: Store 06 running about 18% below the 14-store average, and Outdoor Cooking as the fastest-growing category, consistently across most stores. I'm treating these very differently — one store, one week is weak evidence; a pattern repeating across 13 independent locations is much stronger — and I've set a concrete 4-week re-check on the Store 06 number rather than letting it sit unverified.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've done the first real read of live data, not just confirmed it loaded correctly. Two findings are being raised to the VP with appropriate confidence levels attached, and we've got a specific follow-up date set for the one that needs more data before anyone acts on it.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The first week of real data already surfaced something worth knowing: Outdoor Cooking looks like a genuine growth category across almost every store, which is worth a conversation with merchandising. We're also flagging Store 06's numbers to watch, though it's too early after one week to draw a firm conclusion — we'll have a clearer answer in a few more weeks.

lessons.title: When the Data Surfaces an Uncomfortable Truth
lessons.summary: Handling a finding the stakeholder didn't expect and may not want to hear.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Four weeks in, the Store 06 trend from Lesson 20 hasn't resolved — it's gotten more specific and more uncomfortable. The data now shows Store 06's employee discount line running at roughly 9% of gross sales, against a 14-store average of about 1.5%. This lesson is about handling a finding that points toward a sensitive, human conclusion — without the dashboard, or you, overstating what the data can actually prove.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you're keeping score during a game and you notice one player's numbers look strange — way higher than everyone else's, in a way that doesn't quite add up. You wouldn't run over and accuse them of cheating. You'd quietly tell the coach what you noticed in the numbers and let the coach decide what to look into, because your job was to count accurately, not to decide what the count means about a person.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the point where a BI developer's job quietly collides with a people-management and possibly an HR/loss-prevention issue, and the professional discipline is to report the pattern precisely while explicitly declining to draw the conclusion the pattern seems to suggest. The data shows a fact: Store 06's employee discount line is roughly 9% of gross sales over four weeks, against a company-wide average of 1.5%, and that gap has been consistent across all four weeks, not a one-time spike — which rules out the "noisy single week" explanation that limited the confidence of Lesson 20's finding.

What the data does not show, and what you should not claim it shows, is why — it could be discount-code misuse, a well-intentioned but incorrect employee discount policy specific to that store, a data entry pattern unique to that store's POS terminal configuration, or something else entirely. The deliverable here is a precise, fact-only written note escalated to the VP of Operations — who has the organizational standing and context to decide whether this goes to loss prevention, HR, or a simple manager conversation — not a conclusion, an accusation, or a dashboard annotation visible to anyone outside that reporting line. Getting this handoff right is as much a part of the job as any DAX measure: overstating the finding risks a false accusation with real consequences for someone's job; understating or burying it because it's uncomfortable risks letting a real problem continue.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm the pattern is real and sustained before raising it at all

```sql
SELECT s.store_name,
       SUM(f.employee_discount_amount) / SUM(f.gross_amount) AS discount_rate
FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
JOIN dw.dim_date d  ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE d.full_date BETWEEN @FourWeeksAgo AND @Today
GROUP BY s.store_name
ORDER BY discount_rate DESC;
```

Store 06: 9.1%. Average of the other 13 stores: 1.4%. Check it week by week, not just as a four-week total, to confirm this isn't one unusual week dragging the average:

```sql
SELECT d.fiscal_week, s.store_name,
       SUM(f.employee_discount_amount) / SUM(f.gross_amount) AS weekly_discount_rate
FROM dw.fact_sales f
JOIN dw.dim_store s ON s.store_key = f.store_key
JOIN dw.dim_date d  ON d.date_key = f.date_key
WHERE s.store_id = 'ST06' AND d.full_date BETWEEN @FourWeeksAgo AND @Today
GROUP BY d.fiscal_week, s.store_name
ORDER BY d.fiscal_week;
```

All four weeks independently show 7-11% -- consistent, not a spike. This is what elevates it from "worth watching" (Lesson 20's language) to "worth escalating now."

## Step 2 — Separate what the data shows from what it might mean -- in writing, to yourself, first

```
WHAT THE DATA SHOWS (fact):
  Store 06's employee-discount-to-gross-sales ratio has run 6-7x the
  company average, consistently, for four straight weeks.

WHAT THE DATA DOES NOT SHOW (not fact -- do not state these as findings):
  - Whether this is misuse of the employee discount
  - Whether this is a manager-level policy difference at that store
  - Whether this is a POS configuration or training issue
  - Whether any specific individual is involved
```

## Step 3 — Write the escalation note using only the first list

```
TO: VP of Operations
RE: Store 06 -- employee discount rate, 4-week pattern

Over the last four weeks, Store 06's employee discount amount has
averaged 9.1% of gross sales, compared to a 1.4% average across the
other 13 stores. The pattern is consistent week over week, not driven
by a single unusual week.

I don't have visibility into why -- it could be anything from a
policy difference to a training or system issue to something that
needs a closer look. I wanted to flag the pattern itself now, with the
numbers behind it, so you can decide how you'd like to look into it.

Attached: the week-by-week breakdown behind this number.
```

Notice this note never uses words like "fraud," "misuse," "suspicious," or any language that assigns intent -- it reports a ratio and a trend, full stop.

## Step 4 — Route it to the right person, privately, not to a dashboard or a group channel

Send this directly to the VP of Operations, not as a comment on the shared dashboard and not in a channel visible to Store 06's staff. The VP has the organizational context and authority to decide the next step -- looping in loss prevention, HR, or simply asking the store manager a direct question -- and that decision is explicitly not yours to make from the BI seat.

## Step 5 — If asked your opinion directly, still hold the line

If the VP asks "what do you think is going on," the honest, professional answer is still a version of "I can tell you the number is real and consistent — I can't tell you the cause from this data alone, and I don't want to guess at something with this much consequence for someone's job." Resist the pull to speculate even informally; a casual guess in a hallway conversation can travel much further than it was meant to.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Confirmed Store 06's employee discount rate has run 6-7x the company average consistently across four separate weeks, not a one-time spike — verified week by week before escalating anything. Wrote the finding up as a fact-only ratio and trend, with explicit language that the data doesn't show cause, and sent it directly and privately to the VP of Operations rather than surfacing it anywhere more visible.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: A sensitive finding came up in the data — a sustained anomaly at one store — and we handled it the right way: verified it thoroughly first, then escalated it privately to the one person with the standing to decide what happens next, without speculating about cause or involving anyone else prematurely.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found a real, sustained pattern at Store 06 worth your attention, and we're bringing it to you directly and privately rather than guessing at an explanation or raising it more broadly. What to do next is exactly the kind of judgment call that belongs with you, not with a report.

lessons.title: Presenting the Finished Platform to Stakeholders
lessons.summary: Walking Riverside's leadership team through what was built and why, in their language.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Everything is built, validated, and reconciled. This lesson is the final stakeholder presentation — walking Riverside's leadership team through what was actually delivered, in their language, closing the loop all the way back to the one-page brief from Lesson 1. This is as much a deliverable as any SQL table in this series: a project that's technically finished but poorly presented can still land as a disappointment.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine spending weeks building an amazing treehouse, and then just texting your friend "it's done, come look whenever." They might walk up, glance at it, and miss half the cool features you built in. Now imagine instead you give them a short tour: "Here's the ladder I added so it's safer, here's the window I put where you asked, here's the thing I didn't get to yet and why." The treehouse is the same either way — but the second version makes sure the work actually gets seen and appreciated for what it is.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A good final presentation is structured around the stakeholder's original problem, not around your build order — leading with "here's how we solved what you told us in Lesson 1," not "here's a tour of four pieces of software." The structure that works: restate the original pain point (the Monday spreadsheet rebuild and its typo risk), show the acceptance criteria from Lesson 2 and confirm each one as met with its actual verification evidence (the Lesson 18 reconciliation worksheet, the Lesson 6 schedule-adherence log), do a short live demo hitting both audiences (open the SSRS report as a store manager would, then the Power BI dashboard as the VP would), and close with the v2 backlog from Lesson 3 framed as "what's next," not "what we didn't finish."

Anticipate the two questions that come up in nearly every BI project handoff: "what happens if it breaks" (answer: Lesson 7's alerting design, demonstrated, not just described) and "how do I know these numbers are right" (answer: the Lesson 18 reconciliation process, shown with real numbers, not asserted). Walking in with both of those already answered, unprompted, is what makes a presentation land as confident rather than defensive.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Structure the presentation around their problem, not your build order

```
1. The problem we started with (30 seconds)
2. What we agreed to deliver -- the acceptance criteria (1 minute)
3. Live demo: the store manager's report (2 minutes)
4. Live demo: the VP's dashboard (3 minutes)
5. How we know the numbers are right -- reconciliation (2 minutes)
6. What happens if something breaks -- alerting (1 minute)
7. What's next -- the v2 backlog (2 minutes)
8. Questions
```

## Step 2 — Open with their own words from Lesson 1, not yours

```
"Eight weeks ago, your regional manager was spending most of a Monday
rebuilding a spreadsheet by hand from 14 stores' exports, and that
number wasn't ready until Tuesday afternoon. That's the problem we
set out to solve."
```

## Step 3 — Walk the acceptance criteria as a checklist, with evidence, not assertions

```
AC-2: Load completes before 7:00am.
  EVIDENCE: 30 consecutive nights of SQL Server Agent job history,
  average completion 2:14am, zero misses.

AC-7: Dashboard totals reconcile to source within $0.01.
  EVIDENCE: Reconciliation worksheet (Lesson 18) across 4 test cases,
  all matched exactly.
```

Showing the actual evidence, even briefly, carries far more weight than saying "yes, that's done."

## Step 4 — Run both live demos, each from the actual user's point of view

For the SSRS demo, open the report the way a store manager would -- from the emailed subscription, not from Report Builder's developer view. For the Power BI demo, open the published dashboard and actually click into a store via drill-through live, rather than describing that the feature exists.

## Step 5 — Proactively answer "what if it breaks" and "how do we know it's right" before anyone asks

```
"One more thing before we move to what's next: if a store's file is
ever late or malformed, the system catches it and alerts our team
automatically rather than silently showing incomplete numbers -- you
won't be the one to discover a data problem. And every number on this
dashboard has been traced back, by hand, to the original store export
it came from, across several different kinds of days, to confirm it
matches exactly."
```

## Step 6 — Present the v2 backlog as momentum, not a list of leftovers

```
"This phase was scoped deliberately to sales and inventory, so we could
ship something solid on time. Labor-hours analysis and marketing
attribution are both strong candidates for a next phase -- happy to
scope that whenever you're ready."
```

## Step 7 — Close by handing over, not just presenting

End with a concrete next step: "I'll follow this presentation with the handoff documentation [Lesson 23] so your team has everything needed to maintain this going forward." That sentence previews the very next lesson and signals the engagement is ending responsibly, not abruptly.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran the final stakeholder walkthrough structured around the original acceptance criteria, with real evidence behind each one — job history for the freshness requirement, the reconciliation worksheet for accuracy — rather than just asserting things were done. Demoed both the SSRS report and the Power BI dashboard live, from each audience's actual point of view, and proactively covered failure handling and data accuracy before being asked.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Delivered the final presentation to Riverside's leadership, walking through every item from the original acceptance criteria with evidence it was met, plus live demos of both deliverables. Closed with the v2 backlog framed as next steps, which sets up a clean conversation about a follow-on phase instead of leaving things ambiguous.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We presented the finished platform to the client, demonstrated both deliverables live, and proved — with real numbers, not just claims — that everything in the original agreement was met. They also now have a clear, positive view of what a second phase could include, which sets up a strong case for continued work.

lessons.title: Writing the Handoff Documentation
lessons.summary: Leaving behind documentation someone else could actually maintain this with.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This is the last video in the series: the handoff documentation that lets someone else — a future hire, a different contractor, Riverside's own IT team — actually maintain this platform without you. A platform nobody but its original builder can operate isn't really finished; this lesson closes that gap with a concrete, specific set of documents, not a vague "it's all pretty self-explanatory" note.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you build a really nice treehouse for a family, and then you move away. If you just leave, the next time something squeaks or a board comes loose, nobody will know how to fix it without tearing into it blindly. But if you leave behind a simple notebook — "this board was tricky, tighten this bolt every few months, here's who to call about the roof" — the family can take care of it themselves for years. This lesson is writing that notebook for Riverside's reporting system.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Handoff documentation has a specific job: letting someone who did not build the system diagnose and fix a problem at 2am without calling you. That constraint shapes what belongs in it — not a tour of every design decision made across this series, but the specific, operational information someone actually needs under pressure: where things live, how to restart a failed piece, and what's a known, already-understood issue versus a new problem.

The documents that matter most for Riverside are a data dictionary (what every warehouse column means, including the exact sales definition from Lesson 1 so nobody "fixes" the net sales calculation back to something wrong), an ERD of the star schema, an SSIS operations runbook (the nightly schedule from Lesson 6, the failure modes and their handling from Lesson 7, and concretely how to re-run a failed night using the idempotent load from Lesson 13), an SSRS report catalog (what each parameter does, where subscriptions are configured), and a Power BI refresh and access document (the schedule, the service account, who has edit access). A "known issues" section — explicitly including the Lesson 17 bug and its fix, and the Lesson 19 performance fix — is worth including deliberately: it proves the system has already been through real troubleshooting, and it saves a future maintainer from re-diagnosing something that's already understood.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the data dictionary first, since every other document depends on it being right

```
TABLE: dw.fact_sales
  GRAIN: One row per store, per product, per calendar day.
  net_sales_amount = gross_amount - return_amount - employee_discount_amount
    (Confirmed with Riverside Finance, Lesson 1 -- do not change this
    formula without re-confirming with Finance first.)

TABLE: dw.dim_product
  Type 2 slowly changing dimension. A price or category change creates
  a NEW row with a new product_key and expires the old one -- it does
  NOT update the existing row. This preserves historical pricing for
  year-over-year comparisons.
```

## Step 2 — Draw the ERD and keep it next to the dictionary

A simple star diagram: `fact_sales` in the center, lines to `dim_date`, `dim_store`, `dim_product`, with the join columns labeled on each line. This single picture answers "how does this all fit together" faster than any amount of written description.

## Step 3 — Write the SSIS operations runbook as a troubleshooting checklist, not a narrative

```
SCHEDULE: SQL Server Agent job "Riverside Nightly ETL," 1:15am daily.
  Steps: 01_Extract -> 02_Transform -> 03_Load.

IF A NIGHT FAILS:
  1. Check stg.etl_run_log for the failed stage and message.
  2. Check stg.load_errors and stg.dim_product_unmatched /
     stg.dim_store_unmatched for the specific rows involved.
  3. Fix the underlying issue (e.g. add a missing SKU to dim_product).
  4. Re-run the affected package(s) for that date. The Load package
     is idempotent (deletes-then-inserts scoped to the one date being
     loaded) -- it is SAFE to re-run without creating duplicates.

ALERTING: Failures email data-platform-alerts@riversideoutfitters.com.
```

## Step 4 — Write the SSRS report catalog

```
REPORT: Store Daily Sales (01_StoreDailySales.rdl)
  PARAMETER: @StoreId -- hidden; supplied by subscription, not entered
             by the user.
  SUBSCRIPTIONS: 14 data-driven subscriptions, one per store, 7:30am
             daily. Managed in Report Manager under
             Subscriptions > Data-driven.
  TO ADD A NEW STORE: add a row to dw.dim_store, then add a
             corresponding row to the subscription's driving query.
```

## Step 5 — Write the Power BI refresh and access document

```
DATASET: Riverside_Executive_Dashboard
  REFRESH: Scheduled, 7:15am daily, via the on-premises data gateway
           service account (credentials in Riverside's password vault,
           not in this document).
  ACCESS: VP of Operations has Build + view access to the workspace.
          Report is NOT broadly shared -- it contains all 14 stores'
          data, including the Store 06 pattern discussed in Lesson 21.
```

## Step 6 — Write the known issues section, honestly

```
RESOLVED DURING BUILD:
  - Product Lookup no-match rows were silently lost for several nights
    due to a downstream schema mismatch in the error table and a
    missing FailParentOnError setting. Fixed [date]. See the row-
    accounting check in stg (Step 8, Lesson 17) for the regression
    test now in place.
  - A DAX measure (Total Units Sold) using a row-by-row FILTER(ALL(...))
    pattern caused slow drill-through performance. Rewritten to use
    CALCULATE(SUM(...)) relying on model relationships. Fixed [date].

OPEN / WATCHING:
  - Store 06's employee discount rate pattern, escalated to the VP of
    Operations [date] -- see Lesson 21. Resolution owned by the VP, not
    by this platform.
```

## Step 7 — Package it and hand it over with a short walkthrough, not just a file drop

Compile the data dictionary, ERD, SSIS runbook, SSRS catalog, and Power BI access document into one shared location Riverside's IT team already uses (not your own personal drive), and schedule a 30-minute walkthrough with whoever will actually own this day-to-day -- reading a handoff document alone is not the same as someone being confident they can use it under pressure.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Finalized the handoff package: data dictionary (including the net-sales formula and the dim_product Type 2 behavior, both flagged as 'don't change without re-confirming'), an ERD, an SSIS runbook with explicit re-run steps since the load is idempotent, the SSRS report/subscription catalog, and the Power BI refresh and access document — plus an honest known-issues section covering both the Lesson 17 and Lesson 19 fixes. Walked it through live with Riverside's IT contact rather than just sending the files.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The project closes with a complete handoff package so Riverside's own team can maintain this without needing us on call indefinitely. Every piece — data definitions, how to recover from a failed night, how reports and the dashboard are configured — is documented and was walked through live with their team.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The project is fully handed off. Riverside's own team now has everything needed to run and maintain this independently, including a clear, honest record of two issues we found and fixed during our own testing — so there are no surprises waiting for them after we're gone.
